questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has a 1 week history of unsteadiness when walking and slurred speech. Two years ago she lost vision in her right eye for 6 weeks, which recovered fully. On examination she has a right-sided intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia and horizontal nystagmus. The right optic disc is pale.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Two separate episodes (previous optic neuritis, now an asymmetric cerebellar syndrome) in a young woman show dissemination in time and space.

clues: Two years ago she lost vision in her right eye
The right optic disc is pale
steps.x: A young woman with two CNS episodes at different times and in different places: previous optic neuritis (pale disc) and now a one-sided cerebellar syndrome.

elim: Affects the midline (gait) symmetrically and does not explain a previous episode of visual loss with a pale disc.
Starts in childhood or adolescence and progresses steadily, with areflexia, not discrete episodes.
Sudden onset in an older patient with vascular risk; does not explain an earlier recovered optic neuritis.
Causes a symmetrical posterior column and peripheral neuropathy, not an asymmetric cerebellar syndrome.

steps.x: C: Multiple sclerosis. Lesions separated in time and space in a young woman = MS.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 4 day history of blurred vision in her left eye and an ache behind the eye when she looks to the side. Visual acuity is 6/6 in the right eye and 6/24 in the left eye. Eye movements are full. When a light is swung from the right eye to the left eye, both pupils appear to dilate.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on further examination of the left eye?
o: Halos around lights with a red eye
questions.e: Optic neuritis, the most common presentation of MS, causes painful eye movements, reduced acuity, a relative afferent pupillary defect and colour desaturation (especially red).

clues: blurred vision in her left eye
ache behind the eye when she looks to the side
steps.x: Painful eye movement, reduced acuity and a left relative afferent pupillary defect (the swinging light test) mean left optic neuritis.

elim: Seen in central retinal artery occlusion: sudden painless loss of vision, not painful eye movement.
Suggests a third nerve palsy; eye movements would be impaired.
Central retinal vein occlusion causes painless loss of vision in older patients with vascular risk.
Acute angle-closure glaucoma, with a painful red eye and a fixed mid-dilated pupil.

steps.x: E: Reduced red colour perception. Optic neuritis: pain on eye movement, RAPD and colour desaturation.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has a 2 week history of numbness and tingling spreading up both legs. She was born in Norway and moved to the UK aged 10. She had glandular fever at 16. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and has migraines without aura. MRI shows periventricular white matter lesions.
questions.q: Which feature of her history is most strongly associated with the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Previous Epstein-Barr virus infection (glandular fever) is a key risk factor for MS, together with female sex, age 20 to 40 and Northern European ancestry.

steps.x: Sensory symptoms and periventricular lesions in a young Northern European woman suggest MS; EBV is the infection linked to it.

elim: Raises the risk of venous thrombosis, not of CNS demyelination.
A common primary headache with no link to demyelinating disease.
Northern European ancestry is the risk; moving here is not itself a risk.
Not mentioned and not a recognised association.

steps.x: B: Glandular fever at 16. EBV (glandular fever) is the classic risk factor for MS.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has multiple sclerosis. Over 5 years she has had three separate episodes: right optic neuritis, numbness of her left arm, and unsteadiness of gait. Each came on over a few days, lasted several weeks and then recovered completely. Between episodes she has no symptoms and her neurological examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely disease course?
questions.e: Discrete relapses with full recovery between them is relapsing-remitting MS, the most common disease course.

clues: Between episodes she has no symptoms
steps.x: Separate attacks, each followed by full recovery, with a normal examination in between.

elim: Describes a single first episode; she has had three.
Steady progression from onset without discrete relapses.
MRI lesions found by chance in someone with no symptoms.
Disability that gradually builds between or without relapses after an earlier relapsing phase; she recovers completely.

steps.x: D: Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. Relapses with full recovery = relapsing-remitting MS, the most common course.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with multiple sclerosis has a 5 day history of double vision when looking to the right. MRI shows a new lesion in the left medial longitudinal fasciculus in the pons. Her pupils are equal and reactive and there is no ptosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her eye movements when she looks to the right?
o: Both eyes fail to look to the right
Left eye fails to adduct and right eye has nystagmus
Right eye fails to adduct and left eye has nystagmus
questions.e: A left MLF lesion gives a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia: on right gaze the left eye cannot adduct and the abducting right eye shows nystagmus.

clues: double vision when looking to the right
steps.x: An MLF lesion stops the eye on the same side adducting; the opposite, abducting eye shows nystagmus.

elim: A horizontal gaze palsy from a pontine gaze centre or sixth nerve nucleus lesion, not an MLF lesion.
A left sixth nerve palsy, and would cause diplopia on looking left.
This is a right MLF lesion; the lesion is on the left.
Does not cause horizontal diplopia and is not the MLF pattern.

steps.x: C: Left eye fails to adduct and right eye has nystagmus. INO: the side of the lesion is the eye that fails to adduct.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis notices that her legs become weak and her vision blurs after a hot bath or exercise in the gym. The symptoms go away within an hour of cooling down. Her neurological examination is otherwise unchanged and an MRI shows no new lesions.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of these symptoms?
o: Heat further slows conduction in demyelinated axons
Sodium loss in sweat causing hyponatraemia
questions.e: Uhthoff's phenomenon: demyelinated axons are very temperature sensitive, so heat transiently worsens already impaired conduction.

clues: after a hot bath or exercise
go away within an hour of cooling down
steps.x: Old symptoms briefly return with heat and settle on cooling, with no new lesion: Uhthoff's phenomenon.

elim: Would cause sweating and confusion, and is not linked to old demyelinated pathways.
A relapse lasts more than 24 hours and the MRI shows no new lesions.
Would cause presyncope rather than a return of old MS symptoms.
Does not resolve within an hour of cooling and would not be focal.

steps.x: A: Heat further slows conduction in demyelinated axons. Heat slows conduction in demyelinated nerves; this is not a relapse.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has a 2 week history of numbness in both legs and needing to rush to the toilet to pass urine. Eight months ago she had painful blurred vision in her left eye that recovered. Her legs have increased tone, brisk reflexes and extensor plantar responses.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Electric shock sensation down the limbs on neck flexion
questions.e: Lhermitte's sign (tingling or electric shocks in the limbs on neck flexion) points to a cervical cord demyelinating lesion in MS.

clues: rush to the toilet to pass urine
painful blurred vision in her left eye
steps.x: Previous optic neuritis plus a cord syndrome with bladder urgency and upper motor neurone signs: MS.

elim: A lower motor neurone sign; she has upper motor neurone signs.
A lower motor neurone sign of motor neurone disease, not demyelination.
A peripheral neuropathy pattern, not a cord or brain lesion.
Suggests lumbar nerve root irritation, which gives lower motor neurone signs.

steps.x: B: Electric shock sensation down the limbs on neck flexion. Lhermitte's sign = cervical cord lesion, classic in MS.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man is diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis after a 3 week episode of weakness in his right leg. A second relapse with arm weakness followed 4 months later. MRI shows 15 lesions in the brain and spinal cord. He asks about his outlook.
questions.q: Which feature of his presentation is most associated with a worse prognosis?
o: Complete recovery after the first relapse
questions.e: Older age, male sex, motor signs at onset, early relapses, many MRI lesions and axonal loss all predict a worse prognosis; men do worse overall.

steps.x: He has several poor prognostic factors: older, male, motor onset, an early second relapse and many lesions. Only motor onset is offered.

elim: Full recovery is a good sign, not a bad one.
Sensory or optic onset carries a better outlook; he had motor onset.
A relapsing-remitting course has a better prognosis than primary progressive.
Sensory onset is linked to a better prognosis.

steps.x: B: Motor weakness at onset. Motor onset predicts a worse outlook; sensory or optic onset a better one.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has had secondary progressive multiple sclerosis for 15 years and uses a wheelchair. Over 2 months she has felt low, lost interest in seeing friends, wakes at 4am and has stopped eating well. She has no new weakness, sensory change or visual symptoms. Her TSH is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Depression is a common complication of progressive MS alongside bladder dysfunction and cognitive impairment; low mood, anhedonia and early waking fit.

steps.x: Low mood, anhedonia and early morning waking without new neurology in long-standing MS.

elim: There are no new focal neurological symptoms.
Her TSH is normal.
Is a brief heat-related return of old symptoms, not a 2 month mood change.
Would cause urinary symptoms, fever or a sudden worsening of function.

steps.x: B: Depression complicating multiple sclerosis. Depression is a common complication of progressive MS; screen for it.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has had numbness of her left arm for 10 days. Her neurologist uses the McDonald criteria. MRI brain with gadolinium shows a gadolinium-enhancing periventricular lesion and a non-enhancing juxtacortical lesion, both T2 hyperintense. She has had no previous neurological episodes.
questions.q: Which feature of this MRI shows dissemination in time?
questions.e: An enhancing lesion is active (new) while a non-enhancing lesion is older, so both on one scan show lesions formed at different times; different sites show dissemination in space.

steps.x: One clinical episode, but the scan shows one new (enhancing) and one old (non-enhancing) lesion.

elim: Size does not tell you when lesions formed.
Typical of MS plaques but says nothing about timing.
Location shows dissemination in space, not time.
All MS plaques are T2 hyperintense, old or new.

steps.x: A: Enhancing and non-enhancing lesions together. Enhancing plus non-enhancing lesion = dissemination in time; different sites = space.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has a 3 week history of tingling in her right arm. A year ago she had weakness of her left leg for a month that recovered. Her temperature is 36.8°C and BP 118/76 mmHg. On examination the left leg has brisk reflexes and an extensor plantar response. Sensation is reduced in the right arm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Two episodes affecting different parts of the CNS a year apart, with persisting upper motor neurone signs, in a young woman: MS.

clues: A year ago she had weakness of her left leg
steps.x: Different CNS sites at different times, with upper motor neurone and sensory signs.

elim: Does not produce objective upper motor neurone signs such as an extensor plantar.
An ascending lower motor neurone weakness with areflexia, not brisk reflexes.
Aura lasts under an hour and leaves no signs.
Has no sensory symptoms and does not remit.

steps.x: E: Multiple sclerosis. Dissemination in time and space in a young woman = MS.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis had an episode of painful loss of vision in her right eye 6 months ago, treated with steroids. Her vision has improved but colours still look washed out in that eye. Visual acuity is 6/9 on the right.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on fundoscopy of the right eye?
questions.e: After optic neuritis the disc becomes pale (optic atrophy) from demyelination and later axonal loss, with persistent colour desaturation.

clues: painful loss of vision in her right eye 6 months ago
steps.x: Months after optic neuritis, with persistent colour desaturation.

elim: Seen in hypertensive or diabetic retinopathy and HIV, not after optic neuritis.
A sign of chronic glaucoma, which is painless and slowly progressive.
A feature of age-related macular degeneration.
Papilloedema or acute papillitis, not 6 months later.

steps.x: D: Pale optic disc. Old optic neuritis leaves a pale disc (optic atrophy).

questions.stem: A 32 year old man has had numbness of both legs for 2 weeks. Two years ago he had double vision for a month. MRI shows several periventricular white matter lesions. A lumbar puncture is performed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding in the cerebrospinal fluid?
o: Albuminocytological dissociation with very high protein
IgG oligoclonal bands present in CSF, absent in serum
Raised lymphocytes with low glucose and raised protein
questions.e: Oligoclonal bands (distinct IgG bands) in CSF but not in serum show immune activity inside the CNS and support MS.

clues: Two years ago he had double vision
steps.x: Episodes separated in time and space with periventricular plaques: MS. The CSF shows intrathecal IgG.

elim: Classic of Guillain-Barré syndrome, a peripheral nerve disease.
Bacterial meningitis, with fever and neck stiffness.
Tuberculous meningitis, with fever and weeks of headache.
Shows subarachnoid haemorrhage after a thunderclap headache.

steps.x: B: IgG oligoclonal bands present in CSF, absent in serum. MS CSF: oligoclonal bands unique to the CSF.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has an 8 day history of unsteadiness and numbness of her right hand. Ten months ago she had an episode of tingling in both legs that lasted 3 weeks. She is referred to neurology for the gold standard test for the most likely diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on that investigation?
questions.e: MRI brain and spinal cord with contrast is the gold standard for MS and shows periventricular demyelinating plaques that are T2 hyperintense.

clues: unsteadiness and numbness of her right hand
steps.x: Two episodes in different places at different times: MS. The gold standard is contrast MRI brain and spinal cord.

elim: A feature of Huntington's disease.
A CT sign of acute ischaemic stroke.
Suggests an abscess or tumour.
A feature of Alzheimer's disease.

steps.x: C: Periventricular T2 hyperintense plaques. MRI in MS: periventricular T2 hyperintense plaques, some enhancing.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman has had numbness of her face and left arm for a week. MRI brain with contrast shows one periventricular lesion only, which is enhancing. Her neurologist suspects multiple sclerosis but the scan alone does not meet the diagnostic criteria.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to support the diagnosis?
questions.e: When MRI does not show dissemination in time, CSF oligoclonal bands support the diagnosis of MS.

clues: does not meet the diagnostic criteria
steps.x: MS is suspected but the scan alone is not enough: look for intrathecal IgG.

elim: Much less sensitive than MRI for demyelination; adds nothing.
Used for seizures, not demyelination.
Test peripheral nerves; MS is a CNS disease.
Test for myasthenia gravis.

steps.x: C: Lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands. Equivocal MRI: lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with multiple sclerosis has a 3 month history of passing urine frequently, a weak stream and a feeling that her bladder has not emptied. Urine dipstick is negative for leucocytes and nitrites. She asks whether anything can be done.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Bladder ultrasound for post-void residual volume
questions.e: Bladder dysfunction is a common complication of MS; ultrasound for a post-void residual is the first test to assess emptying.

steps.x: Incomplete emptying in MS without infection.

elim: Looks for stones, not bladder emptying.
Invasive and used for haematuria or suspected tumour.
Bladder dysfunction is expected in MS; the first step is to measure emptying.
A later, more invasive test if simple assessment does not explain symptoms.

steps.x: A: Bladder ultrasound for post-void residual volume. MS bladder symptoms: ultrasound for post-void residual first.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with a 30 year history of multiple sclerosis dies from aspiration pneumonia. In her final years she had severe fixed disability. Sections of the brain and spinal cord are examined at post-mortem.
questions.q: Which is the most likely histological finding?
o: Lewy bodies in the substantia nigra
Plaques of demyelination with axonal loss
questions.e: The pathological hallmark of MS is plaques of demyelination with eventual axonal loss, which explains permanent disability.

steps.x: Long-standing MS with fixed disability.

elim: The hallmark of Alzheimer's disease.
The hallmark of Parkinson's disease.
Seen in neurosarcoidosis.
Seen in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

steps.x: D: Plaques of demyelination with axonal loss. MS histology: demyelinating plaques, with axonal loss in late disease.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 2 day history of painful blurred vision in her right eye. Visual acuity is 6/36 on the right. There is a right relative afferent pupillary defect. She has never had neurological symptoms before. Her GP asks what imaging will show whether she is likely to develop multiple sclerosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: In optic neuritis, urgent contrast MRI brain looks for other central demyelinating lesions, which support dissemination in space and predict MS.

clues: painful blurred vision in her right eye
steps.x: First episode of optic neuritis: look for silent brain lesions.

elim: Will not show small demyelinating plaques.
Does not assess the brain for other lesions.
May be added in atypical cases but does not look for central demyelination.
Used for giant cell arteritis in people over 50.

steps.x: E: Urgent MRI brain with contrast. Optic neuritis: urgent MRI brain with contrast.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis has a 5 day history of weakness of her right leg. She now needs a stick to walk. She has no fever and her urine dipstick is negative. Her vision is normal. The neurology team confirms an acute relapse.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: Acute MS relapses are treated with high-dose oral methylprednisolone, discussed with a specialist, once infection has been excluded.

steps.x: A disabling relapse without infection or visual involvement.

elim: Used in Guillain-Barré syndrome and myasthenic crisis, not MS relapses.
A long-term disease-modifying drug; it does not treat the current relapse.
Treats spasticity, not the relapse itself.
Not first line for a typical relapse.

steps.x: A: High-dose oral methylprednisolone. MS relapse: high-dose oral methylprednisolone (IV if optic neuritis).

questions.stem: A 38 year old man with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis has a 3 day history of pain on moving his left eye and loss of central vision. Visual acuity is 6/60 in the left eye with a left relative afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy is normal. His temperature is 36.9°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: An acute MS relapse with optic neuritis is treated initially with IV methylprednisolone.

clues: pain on moving his left eye
steps.x: Optic neuritis (painful eye movements, RAPD, normal disc acutely) in known MS.

elim: Reduces future relapses; it does not treat this one.
Treats herpes infection; there is no rash or retinitis.
Too low a dose to treat a relapse.
Treats bacterial conjunctivitis, not optic nerve inflammation.

steps.x: C: IV methylprednisolone. MS relapse with optic neuritis: IV methylprednisolone.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. She has had two relapses in the past 2 years, both recovered well, and she walks unaided. She is not on any regular treatment and asks about medicine to reduce the number of relapses.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term treatment?
questions.e: Interferon beta is a disease-modifying therapy that reduces the long-term relapse rate in RRMS for patients who can walk unaided.

clues: two relapses in the past 2 years
steps.x: Active RRMS in someone who walks unaided, not on a disease-modifying drug.

elim: Treats spasticity; it does not change the disease course.
Treats spasticity or neuropathic pain, not relapse rate.
Steroids treat acute relapses; they are not a long-term preventer.
Long-term steroids do not reduce relapses and cause harm.

steps.x: C: Interferon beta. Interferon beta reduces relapses in RRMS in people able to walk unaided.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman was diagnosed with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis a year ago. She has had three disabling relapses in the past 12 months and MRI shows several new enhancing lesions. She has not yet started any disease-modifying treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate disease-modifying treatment?
questions.e: Natalizumab is first line for highly active RRMS with more than two relapses a year, and second line after first-line failure.

clues: three disabling relapses in the past 12 months
steps.x: Highly active RRMS: more than two relapses in a year with active MRI.

elim: An older immunosuppressant, not a first-line MS disease-modifying drug.
Used in transplant and some autoimmune diseases, not MS.
Used in lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.
Used in rheumatoid arthritis, not MS.

steps.x: E: Natalizumab. Highly active RRMS: natalizumab.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man with secondary progressive multiple sclerosis has stiffness and painful spasms in both legs that stop him sleeping. He has taken baclofen at the maximum tolerated dose for 3 months with only partial benefit and sees a physiotherapist weekly. His urine dipstick is negative.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: MS spasticity is treated with physiotherapy plus baclofen and gabapentin; if baclofen alone is not enough, add gabapentin.

clues: baclofen at the maximum tolerated dose
steps.x: Spasticity only partly helped by baclofen, with physiotherapy already in place.

elim: Treats myasthenia gravis and does not reduce spasticity.
A dopamine agonist for Parkinson's disease or restless legs.
This is chronic spasticity, not an acute relapse.
Physiotherapy is a core part of spasticity management.

steps.x: A: Add gabapentin. MS spasticity: baclofen and gabapentin, with physiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with primary progressive multiple sclerosis has lost 8 kg over 4 months. He has had two aspiration pneumonias this year. A speech and language assessment shows that his swallow is unsafe for all consistencies and this is not expected to recover. He wants to stay at home.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management of his nutrition?
questions.e: When long-term nutritional support is needed and oral intake is unsafe (for example dysphagia in progressive MS), a gastrostomy tube is used.

steps.x: Permanent unsafe swallow with weight loss and aspiration.

elim: Oral intake is unsafe for all consistencies.
Suitable only for short-term feeding.
His swallow is unsafe even with modified consistencies.
Used when the gut does not work; his gut is fine.

steps.x: A: Gastrostomy tube. Long-term unsafe swallow in progressive MS: gastrostomy.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis had a relapse affecting her balance 4 months ago, treated with oral methylprednisolone. She has had no new symptoms since but still has mild unsteadiness and fatigue when walking. She takes interferon beta. MRI shows no new or enhancing lesions.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of her persisting symptoms?
questions.e: Residual symptoms between relapses are managed with physiotherapy and other symptomatic measures, not more steroids.

steps.x: Stable disease with a residual deficit after a treated relapse.

elim: There is no new relapse; steroids do not help residual deficits.
Not used for MS symptoms.
Treats Parkinson's disease, not ataxia.
She has had no further relapses and no new MRI activity.

steps.x: D: Referral for physiotherapy. Residual MS deficit: symptomatic care such as physiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with highly active relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis has had three relapses in the past year and starts natalizumab infusions every 4 weeks. Her neurologist explains how the drug reduces new plaques forming in the brain.
questions.q: Which is the mechanism of action of natalizumab?
o: Blocks leukocyte adhesion molecules on lymphocytes
questions.e: Natalizumab blocks leukocyte adhesion molecules (alpha-4 integrin), so lymphocytes cannot migrate across the blood-brain barrier.

clues: reduces new plaques forming in the brain
steps.x: Plaques form when T cells cross the blood-brain barrier; natalizumab stops them getting in.

elim: This is the action of ocrelizumab, not natalizumab.
This is how baclofen relieves spasticity.
This is pyridostigmine, used in myasthenia gravis.
This is methotrexate.

steps.x: A: Blocks leukocyte adhesion molecules on lymphocytes. Natalizumab: anti-adhesion molecule, stops lymphocytes crossing the BBB.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with multiple sclerosis has numbness of both legs. Evoked potential studies show markedly slowed conduction in central sensory pathways, while peripheral nerve conduction studies are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the slowed conduction?
o: Loss of CNS myelin impairing saltatory conduction
Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra
questions.e: MS is a T-cell-mediated attack on CNS myelin; demyelination slows or blocks saltatory conduction, giving symptoms that depend on lesion site.

clues: slowed conduction in central sensory pathways
peripheral nerve conduction studies are normal
steps.x: Central, not peripheral, conduction is slowed in MS.

elim: Myasthenia gravis, a neuromuscular junction disease.
Motor neurone disease, with no sensory loss.
Peripheral conduction is normal; this is Guillain-Barré syndrome.
Parkinson's disease, a movement disorder.

steps.x: D: Loss of CNS myelin impairing saltatory conduction. MS: CNS demyelination slows saltatory conduction.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman is diagnosed with multiple sclerosis after an episode of optic neuritis and a later spinal cord relapse. She asks which cells in her nervous system are being damaged by her immune system.
questions.q: Which cell type is primarily destroyed?
questions.e: Activated T cells cross the blood-brain barrier and attack oligodendrocytes, the cells that make CNS myelin.

steps.x: Optic nerve and cord are CNS: myelin there is made by oligodendrocytes.

elim: The main target in neuromyelitis optica (aquaporin-4), not MS.
Immune cells of the CNS that take part in inflammation but are not the target.
Cerebellar neurons lost in some paraneoplastic and degenerative ataxias.
Make peripheral myelin, damaged in Guillain-Barré syndrome.

steps.x: C: Oligodendrocytes. MS destroys oligodendrocytes (CNS myelin).

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has had multiple sclerosis for 20 years. In the early years every relapse recovered completely, but over the last 8 years each relapse has left him with more weakness, and he now uses a frame. MRI shows atrophy of the brain and spinal cord.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his permanent disability?
o: Conduction block from oedema around plaques
questions.e: Repeated inflammation and demyelination eventually cause axonal loss (seen as atrophy), which produces permanent disability and a worse prognosis.

clues: atrophy of the brain and spinal cord
steps.x: Recovery early, then fixed deficits with atrophy.

elim: Not the mechanism of MS disability.
Oedema is temporary and explains recovery, not permanent deficit.
Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves; remyelination would improve function.
Uhthoff's phenomenon is temporary.

steps.x: B: Axonal loss after repeated demyelination. Permanent MS disability comes from axonal loss.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has a 3 year history of gradually worsening balance, stiffness of both legs and urinary urgency. She cannot recall any sudden episodes or periods of improvement; things have simply got steadily worse. She has a spastic, ataxic gait. MRI shows spinal cord and periventricular lesions and CSF contains oligoclonal bands.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A monophasic history of steady progression without discrete relapses, with MS findings on MRI and CSF, is primary progressive MS.

steps.x: Progressive from the start, never any relapses, but the scan and CSF show MS.

elim: A single acute episode, not 3 years of steady decline.
Would not produce periventricular plaques and oligoclonal bands.
Has discrete relapses with recovery; she has none.
Follows an earlier relapsing-remitting phase, which she never had.

steps.x: C: Primary progressive multiple sclerosis. Steady progression from onset with no relapses = primary progressive MS.
